article_title: Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation
citation: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013).
title: Ottoman Empire face-to-face debate corpus with hand-coded transactivity
description: A corpus of face-to-face dyadic debates on the cause of the decline of the Ottoman Empire, collected in a laboratory setting for research on arousal and learning. Male undergraduates aged 18 to 25 argued assigned sides using four-page background packets; debates lasted eight minutes under blocked or freeform conditions. As printed, "A total of 76 sessions (with 152 participants) were collected and used for further analysis, half of which were in the freeform condition." Speech was transcribed, segmented into 5490 independent-clause segments, and coded for transactivity; prevalence averaged 36 other-oriented transacts per session (minimum 22, maximum 60).
requirements: Directional microphones per speaker for clean separate-channel speech recording
constraints: Participants did not know each other beforehand and shared gender, age range, and student status, controlling for known accommodation moderators
target_learning_goals: argumentive discussion and knowledge integration in debate
examples: The freeform condition allowed free talking for eight minutes, while the blocked condition gave each speaker two-minute turns
key_sources: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9172-5

article_title: A criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with alternative suggestions.
citation: ARTHUK S. OTIS (Stanford University). (1917). A Criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with Alternative Suggestions. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VIII, No. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Otis+criticism+Yerkes-Bridges+point+scale
title: Otis's absolute grade of intelligence scale with coefficient of brightness
description: The article proposes expressing intelligence on an arbitrary absolute scale whose median adult grade is 100 and whose unit is one-tenth of the quartile of the distribution of absolute degrees, so that adult grades fall in a normal distribution. Brightness is then expressed as a coefficient of brightness: the quotient of a person's absolute grade by the absolute grade normal for his age. Because degrees of brightness are assumed constant for a given child, this "absolute intelligence quotient" lets one predict the probable ultimate absolute grade, and hence maximum attainments, from a child's rank at any age. The article states the scale is "a means to an end," discarded once percentages of persons exceeded are read off.
requirements: Assumes the distribution of absolute grades of intelligence is normal for each age and that degrees of brightness are constant for a given individual
constraints: The exact relation between a child's brightness at one age and another awaits repeated testing of the same children in successive years; the mental-age method cannot express degrees above normal adult ability
target_learners: children of all ages being assessed for intelligence
target_learning_goals: measurement of general intelligence and prediction of ultimate intellectual attainment
examples: The article tabulates theoretical percentages of adults attaining grades 60 to 140 with the quartile taken as 8 points and median at 100, and illustrates a 12-year-old with 880 points on the 75% curve having a coefficient of brightness of 1.10
key_sources: ARTHUK S. OTIS (Stanford University). (1917). A Criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with Alternative Suggestions. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VIII, No. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Otis+criticism+Yerkes-Bridges+point+scale

article_title: A criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with alternative suggestions.
citation: ARTHUK S. OTIS (Stanford University). (1917). A Criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with Alternative Suggestions. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VIII, No. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Otis+criticism+Yerkes-Bridges+point+scale
title: The Binet Point Scale: a paper reorganization of the Stanford Revision giving one point per month of mental age
description: The article constructs a Binet Point Scale by reorganizing the Stanford Revision of the Binet Scale on paper into six lists, each list composed of tests representing different degrees of the same ability, with point values read from a correspondence table in which one point equals one month of mental age. Administration and scoring are identical to the ordinary Binet; only the mode of expression changes, from mental age to a summed point-score. The article argues that "the present Binet Scale is already a point scale, for all the purposes for which Yerkes' and Bridges' alteration of the Binet Scale could be used," and that this conversion preserves more nearly equal point values than the Yerkes-Bridges rearrangement.
requirements: The tests are given and scored exactly as in the regular Binet Scale; the correspondence table assumes passing six tests (12 points) indicates mental age III and twelve tests (24 points) mental age IV
constraints: Point values are only approximately equal, since rate of growth slows near maturity; mental ages XVI and XVIII are fictitious designations
target_learners: children examined with the Binet Scale
target_learning_goals: expressing degree of intellectual maturity as a statistically convenient point-score
examples: The article's Table VII lays out the six lists with point values 2 and 4 per test, and states a point-score of 164 indicates a mental age of fifteen years and eight months
key_sources: ARTHUK S. OTIS (Stanford University). (1917). A Criticism of the Yerkes-Bridges Point Scale, with Alternative Suggestions. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VIII, No. 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Otis+criticism+Yerkes-Bridges+point+scale

article_title: Group Tests of Intelligence. An Annotated List.
citation: Bell, J. C. (1920). Group Tests of Intelligence: An Annotated List. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 103-108. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Otis Group Intelligence Scale Advanced Examination: ten tests, described as the oldest and perhaps most widely used group test
description: Arthur S. Otis's Advanced Examination is described as "The oldest and perhaps the most widely used of the group tests of intelligence", consisting of 10 tests each containing from 20 to 30 tasks, including following directions, opposites, disarranged sentences, proverbs, arithmetic, geometric figures, analogies, similarities, narrative completion and memory, suitable for grades 5 to 12. The Army Alpha examination is noted as based largely on the Otis tests.
requirements: Group administration with printed test booklets; each test contains from 20 to 30 tasks as printed
constraints: Suitable for use in grades 5 to 12 as printed
key_sources: Bell, J. C. (1920). Group Tests of Intelligence: An Annotated List. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 103-108. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0073682

article_title: An absolute point scale for the group measurement of intelligence.- Part II.
citation: Arthur S. Otis. (1917). An Absolute Point Scale for the Group Measurement of Intelligence.—Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Otis Absolute Point Scale (Scale I and Scale II) for group measurement of intelligence
description: The Absolute Point Scale is a group intelligence test composed of ten tests per scale (including Spelling, Arithmetic, Synonyms, Proverbs, Relation, Narrative Completion, Following Directions, Geometric, Disarranged Sentences, and Digits), administered in two parallel forms whose correlation provides the scale's reliability. Scores are expressed on an absolute point scale with grade norms, and inter-test correlations are reported both raw and "corrected for attenuation due to errors of measurement."
requirements: Two parallel forms (Scale I and Scale II) are needed to obtain the double measures from which the reliability coefficient and probable error are computed.
constraints: The author notes the Spelling Test is too easy and the Synonym Test somewhat too easy for the group tested, and that refinement of item difficulty is not of great value until more obvious defects of the scale are eliminated.
target_learning_goals: group measurement of general intelligence and mental age
examples: Applied to 121 pupils across the fourth, sixth, and eighth grades, yielding grade norms of 385, 514, and 605 points and a median score of 500 for the whole group.
key_sources: Arthur S. Otis. (1917). An Absolute Point Scale for the Group Measurement of Intelligence.—Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074753

article_title: A study of association in defectives.
citation: Otis, M. (1915). A Study of Association in Defectives. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VI, No. 5. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Study+of+Association+in+Defectives%22+Otis
title: Five-type classification of word-association responses as an index of mental level or abnormality
description: Otis proposes a taxonomy of association-test responses into five types: repetition of the stimulus, non-logical responses, sound reactions, more-than-one-word reactions, and normal single-word reactions matching the Kent-Rosanoff frequency tables. A child is assigned to a type only when "50 per cent, of a child's reactions must be clearly of a given type to consider the child as belonging to that type," with mixed types otherwise classified by their two most frequent components. The types are interpreted as marking stages of language development from imitation through sentence-thought to single-word analysis, and are examined for diagnostic and age-test value.
requirements: Administration of a standard word list (the Kent-Rosanoff 100-word list) with individually recorded, timed responses so reaction types can be classified per child.
constraints: A child is assigned to a type only when at least 50 per cent of reactions clearly belong to it; otherwise the child is classified as a mixed type.
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of mental status and language-development level through associational tendencies
examples: Illustrative papers are given for each type, e.g. a boy of 11 testing 6-1 for Type I and a Mongolian male of 33 testing 3-4 for Type II.
key_sources: Otis, M. (1915). A Study of Association in Defectives. The Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. VI, No. 5. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Study+of+Association+in+Defectives%22+Otis

article_title: An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I.
citation: Otis, A. S. (1918). An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 9(5), 239-261. https://books.google.com/books/about/the_journal_of_educational_psychology.html
title: The Absolute Point Scale: ten objective tests compiled in duplicate forms for group measurement of general mental ability
description: The scale is a battery of ten tests—Spelling, Arithmetic, Synonyms and Antonyms, Memory for Digits, Proverbs, Disarranged Sentences, Relation, Geometric, Following Directions, and Narrative Completion—compiled in duplicate. As printed: "The scale was compiled in duplicate. There were, in other words, two complete tests of each kind." The two forms of each kind were made as alike as possible without using the same material, and the ideas were drawn chiefly from the Stanford Revision of the Binet Scale, with the remaining tests designed especially for this study.
requirements: Each test exists in two near-identical forms to support reliability estimation
Scoring rules are fixed per test, e.g. one count per correct answer with deductions for incorrect answers on some tests
constraints: The Spelling Test, though a strong measure, was later dropped from the scale
The Disarranged Sentence Test is a speed test requiring fixed time limits
target_learners: pupils in grades 4 to 8 of the elementary school
examples: The Arithmetic Test used 16 problems with easy computation so emphasis fell on reasoning; the Proverb Test asked pupils to match ten proverbs to explaining statements among twelve
key_sources: Otis, A. S. (1918). An absolute point scale for the group measurements of intelligence. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 9(5), 239-261. https://books.google.com/books/about/the_journal_of_educational_psychology.html

article_title: Improving the Competence of Diagrammatic and Argumentative Representation in Physics through Android-Based Mobile Learning Application
citation: Liliarti, N., & Kuswanto, H. (2018). Improving the Competence of Diagrammatic and Argumentative Representation in Physics through Android-based Mobile Learning Application. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 106-122. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1138a
title: Android-based physics learning media built on the othok-othok toy ship
description: An Android application developed with Adobe Flash Professional CS6 and Action Script 3, packaging learning materials on Newton's law, Archimedes' principle, and convective heat transfer around the othok-othok toy ship, a local Yogyakarta toy that "emits a repetitive knocking sound". Its output was "a file with an apk extension which is required for installation in Android". A design matrix organized content by indicators (giving factual content, building an argument, making a diagram before calculation, giving a diagram and building argumentation) across the physics topics, using videos and animations of the toy ship.
requirements: Android device such as a smartphone, tablet, or notebook capable of installing the apk application
constraints: The material used during the experimentation was about Newton's law only
target_learners: first-grade (Grade X) senior high school physics students
target_learning_goals: Newton's law, Archimedes' principle, and convection heat transfer concepts
examples: Experts and physics teachers judged the media feasible; it was field tested with Grade X students at SMA N 3 Yogyakarta
key_sources: Liliarti, N., & Kuswanto, H. (2018). Improving the Competence of Diagrammatic and Argumentative Representation in Physics through Android-based Mobile Learning Application. International Journal of Instruction, 11(3), 106-122. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1138a

article_title: Development of an Instructional Model for Online Task-Based Interactive Listening for EFL Learners
citation: Xingbin Tian & Suksan Suppasetseree. (2013). Development of an Instructional Model for Online Task-Based Interactive Listening for EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n3p30
title: The OTIL Model: a six-phase, 17-step instructional design model for online task-based interactive listening
description: The OTIL Model is a systematic, web-based instructional design model for English listening instruction that combines a task-based approach with interactive online learning. It comprises 6 phases and 17 steps: identify setting, set instructional goals, design lessons, produce the online instructional package, conduct developed lessons, and evaluate. The article states it is "an online interactive listening instruction design with task-based approach" and "a learner-centered instruction design, emphasizing interaction."
requirements: Web-based activities such as Forum, Glossary, Chat, Wiki, and Quiz are required so that learner-instructor, learner-learner and learner-content interaction and immediate feedback are supported
constraints: The model was developed and evaluated for college English listening teaching in China; the experts noted weaknesses in phase names, step explanations and the flow of the model, which were revised
target_learners: second-year non-English major undergraduate EFL learners
examples: The researcher constructed OTIL lessons in Moodle with tasks and activities embedded in Forum, Glossary, Chat and Quiz modules, and taught the experimental class with them
key_sources: Xingbin Tian & Suksan Suppasetseree. (2013). Development of an Instructional Model for Online Task-Based Interactive Listening for EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n3p30

article_title: Development of an Instructional Model for Online Task-Based Interactive Listening for EFL Learners
citation: Xingbin Tian & Suksan Suppasetseree. (2013). Development of an Instructional Model for Online Task-Based Interactive Listening for EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n3p30
title: OTIL lessons delivered through Moodle modules (Forum, Glossary, Chat, Wiki, Quiz)
description: The OTIL lessons are online listening lessons implemented on the Moodle learning management platform, with "learning tasks and activities ... embedded in Moodle modules, such as Forum, Glossary, Chat and Quiz." Moodle was chosen after analyzing the technical environment at Tongren University and offers interactive tools supporting synchronous and asynchronous interaction, collaboration, and automatically corrected exercises with immediate feedback.
requirements: Computers, the Internet or Intranet, network servers, server capabilities, software and hardware meeting minimum requirements, per the learning context analysis step
constraints: The article describes Moodle use in the specific context of college English listening at Tongren University, China
target_learning_goals: English listening comprehension through interactive task-based online activities
examples: Students interacted synchronously in chat rooms and engaged in asynchronous discussions in Wikis and Forums, and online exercises were automatically corrected and graded
key_sources: Xingbin Tian & Suksan Suppasetseree. (2013). Development of an Instructional Model for Online Task-Based Interactive Listening for EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n3p30

article_title: Development of an Instructional Model for Online Task-Based Interactive Listening for EFL Learners
citation: Xingbin Tian & Suksan Suppasetseree. (2013). Development of an Instructional Model for Online Task-Based Interactive Listening for EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n3p30
title: Online listening instruction should be learner-centered and interaction-focused rather than teacher-centered
description: The article argues that listening instruction online should emphasize learner-centered learning and interaction: "The teaching process should emphasize learner-centered learning and learning in interaction." In the OTIL lessons the instructor acted as facilitator while students took more responsibility for learning, interacting with peers and teachers through computer-mediated and face-to-face formats. The authors link this to the significant listening gains of the experimental class.
requirements: An online platform providing multiple interaction formats (synchronous chat, asynchronous forums/wikis) and real-world listening tasks
constraints: The article cites Rivers (2000) that teacher-centered classrooms cannot be interactive classrooms; evidence comes from one quasi-experiment in a Chinese university context
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension and active engagement in learning
examples: In the OTIL lessons students were divided into subgroups, interacted synchronously in chat rooms or engaged in asynchronous discussions in Wikis and Forums, and exchanged information in an online cooperative learning environment
key_sources: Xingbin Tian & Suksan Suppasetseree. (2013). Development of an Instructional Model for Online Task-Based Interactive Listening for EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n3p30

article_title: Postsurgical Otolaryngology Emergencies: A Simulation to Improve Multidisciplinary Patient Care During Rare, Critical Situations.
citation: Neevel Andrew J. MD, Ramazani Fatemeh MD, Vance Kaitlin NP, Leginza Marie NP, Casper Keith A. MD, Thorne Marc C. MD, MPH, Kupfer Robbi A. MD. (2026). Postsurgical Otolaryngology Emergencies: A Simulation to Improve Multidisciplinary Patient Care During Rare, Critical Situations. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11612
title: Multidisciplinary simulation curriculum for carotid blowout and tracheostomy false passage
description: A 2-hour simulation curriculum featuring two 45-minute scenarios on a postoperative head and neck cancer patient, run concurrently in separate rooms with a 15-minute debrief each. It uses "a high-fidelity mannequin, 3D-printed anterior neck, and standard airway equipment" and was designed to improve technical and nontechnical skills of otolaryngology nursing and medical teams managing rare, high-acuity emergencies.
requirements: Participants must have baseline training appropriate to their professional practice; prior airway or head and neck cancer-specific care experience is not required
Two trained facilitators per scenario: one otolaryngology faculty member and one experienced nurse educator, with standardized orientation
constraints: Foundational skills such as tracheostomy tube removal, suction, and initial management of alcohol withdrawal were not separately taught or formally assessed; they were expected baseline competencies
target_learning_goals: Recognize and manage tracheostomy false passage and carotid blowout
Articulate one's role and adjacent team members' roles in postoperative emergencies
Communicate effectively to triage acuity and coordinate team-based management
examples: Scenarios simulated a carotid blowout and a tracheostomy false passage on a postoperative male patient aged 50-60 years following complex ablation and reconstruction for head and neck cancer
key_sources: Neevel Andrew J. MD, Ramazani Fatemeh MD, Vance Kaitlin NP, Leginza Marie NP, Casper Keith A. MD, Thorne Marc C. MD, MPH, Kupfer Robbi A. MD. (2026). Postsurgical Otolaryngology Emergencies: A Simulation to Improve Multidisciplinary Patient Care During Rare, Critical Situations. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11612

article_title: Developing a best practice framework for clinical competency education in the traditional East-Asian medicine curriculum.
citation: Han Sang Yun, Lee Seung-Hee, Chae Han. (2022). Developing a best practice framework for clinical competency education in the traditional East-Asian medicine curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03398-4
title: Office of Traditional Korean Medicine Education as central governance body
description: The Office of Traditional Korean Medicine Education (OTKME) is "the central body of development and evaluation of the curriculum, research on teaching-learning methods, management of human resources, equipment and consumables". It publishes the guidebooks, trains standardized patients, supervises practice facilities, organizes the Clinical Performance Test, supports PBL classes, and manages the CBT web server. It is led by a chairperson and three full-time officers with two steering committees and two quality-improvement committees.
requirements: A chairperson and three full-time officers plus steering and quality committees to oversee curriculum, budget, admission and graduation issues
constraints: The discussion notes "the absence of experts in the OTKME should be improved", recommending staff qualified with research methodology for evidence-based teaching
target_learners: medical students in a traditional Korean medicine program
target_learning_goals: clinical skills and procedures across biomedicine and traditional medicine
examples: The OTKME trains standardized personnel as patients during "15-h scenario training" and operates the CPT test rooms
key_sources: Han Sang Yun, Lee Seung-Hee, Chae Han. (2022). Developing a best practice framework for clinical competency education in the traditional East-Asian medicine curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03398-4
